Foundations of AI: Multi-Agent Systems
This course provides a comprehensive introduction to Artificial Intelligence, covering both foundational concepts and key algorithmic techniques. It begins with an overview of AI and problem-solving using single-agent search methods such as A* search. The course then explores decision-making in adversarial settings through two-agent search techniques, including minimax and alpha-beta pruning.
Building on these foundations, the course introduces sequential decision-making under uncertainty via Markov Decision Processes (MDPs). It further covers learning-based approaches such as Multi-Armed Bandits (MAB) and Reinforcement Learning (RL).
Finally, the course examines strategic interactions in multi-agent systems through game theory and multi-agent reinforcement learning. It focuses on decision-making in competitive and cooperative environments, analyzing how agents’ choices impact outcomes and how equilibrium concepts can guide optimal strategies. Applications span economics, social sciences, and modern AI systems, providing a framework for understanding complex decentralized interactions and designing efficient algorithms.

Topics. 


Till midsem graph theory. Then coding theory as an application of LA.


1. Logic: Propositions, connectives, quantifiers, rules of inference, induction, strong induction, structural induction— examples. 
Rosen book on discrete maths.


2. Combinatorics: Definition of graphs and various structures in graphs. Koenig, Hall, and Menger theorems.
Douglas West.


3.  The TONCAS (The obvious necessary conditions are also sufficient) principle.
Douglas West.


4. Common proof techniques (structural induction, attacking minimal counterexamples, etc.) for graph theory.
Douglas West.


5. algebraic techniques, algorithmic proofs (Havel-Hakimi theorem, Eulerian circuits, Prufer codes).
Douglas West.


Coding theory in Zp — Guruswamy et al (Essential coding theory).


6. Approximation algorithm techniques – LP rounding, SDP rounding, etc.


7. MultiwayCut and k cut. (max flow min cut prereq.)
The multiway cut problem 
The minimum k-cut problem 


8. tree decompositions and dynamic programming (Independent set), algebraic techniques for exact algorithms (inclusion-exclusion).
Tardos. 


9. Probability theory: Review of basics, Expectation and variance, linearity of expectation, concentration bounds, derandomization, probabilistic methods in proofs. Advanced topic: A randomized algorithm for perfect matching.

   15% homeworks + 40% midsem + 45% endsem.


There will be roughly 3-4 homework assignments. 




Textbooks:
1. Vazirani, Approximation algorithms. https://ics.uci.edu/~vazirani/book.pdf

https://www.designofapproxalgs.com/book.pdf 


3. Introduction to graph theory by Douglas B. West.

https://cse.buffalo.edu/faculty/atri/courses/coding-theory/book/


Related topics: 
Computational models: What is computation?, motivation and definition of RAM (Random access machine) model, Algorithmic correctness and worst-case complexity. lower bounds vs upper bounds, reductions, Satisfiability and reductions to Satisfiability (Hamiltonian Cycle to Satisfiability, Vertex Cover to Satisfiability), hardness and completeness via reductions. identifying the right reductions (many-one, Turing, logspace etc.), gadget constructions (one or two advanced examples). Advanced topic: Boolean circuits, constant-depth circuit constructions, circuit reductions.

Incentives and Machine Learning
This course focuses on the intersection of machine learning and mechanism design. It explores how incentives shape the behavior of agents in Machine Learning (ML) environments and how to design algorithms that align incentives with desirable system outcomes. The course aims to discuss how to apply the tools of game theory and mechanism design to problems in ML, such as designing incentive-compatible learning algorithms, managing strategic agents, and optimizing decision-making processes in multi-agent systems

CS691 VIII: Algebraic Complexity Theory
2026-27 Semester I
Summary
Algebraic complexity theory deals with the computation of polynomials using the basic operations addition and multiplication. For example, we can compute the polynomial xy + xz using two multiplications and one addition. By using distributivity, we can perform the same computation as x(y + z) which costs one addition and only one multiplication. The primary goal of algebraic complexity theory is to understand the minimum number of operations for computing interesting polynomials such as determinants and matrix multiplication polynomials (also called the complexity of these polynomials). For example, can we prove that multiplying two n x n matrices can be done using n² operations? (The trivial method uses n 3 operations. We can achieve n^{2 . 37})
In this course, we will first learn about polynomial families such as matrix multiplication polynomials, determinants, and permanents. What makes them interesting is the fact that they seem to characterize the complexity of large classes of interesting polynomials? For example, any polynomial that can be written as a small formula can also be written as a small determinant. We will then look at very clever ways to compute polynomials efficiently such as computing all first-order partial derivatives of an n-variate polynomial using almost the same number of operations as for the polynomial (If you compute them individually, you’ll need about n times more, which is too much)! and the theory underlying Strassen’s fast matrix multiplication algorithm.
Even though we have many clever algorithms to efficiently compute certain important polynomials, there seems to be a lack of techniques that will allow us to prove that certain polynomials are hard to compute, despite our strong suspicion that they actually are hard to compute. Nevertheless, we can impose natural restrictions such as monotonicity (disallow subtraction), constant-depth (limit nesting of operations), multilinearity (disallow squaring variables) and show that under these restrictions, certain polynomials are hard to compute.
Outcomes
This course is an ideal first-course in computational complexity for mathematicians. It is useful if you are trying to transition from core mathematical areas to CS or if you want to get an overview of some research in the intersection of math and CS.


This course is also suitable for students of theoretical CS doing research in algorithms for expanding their view of computation.
Evaluation
The evaluation plan will be determined by the number of registrations.

2. Arithmetic circuits lower-bounds survey, Ramprasad Saptarishi.
3. Fast Matrix Multiplication, Markus Bläser.

ES 607 Foundations of Fluid Dynamics


Description
This is a postgraduate level fluid dynamics course.  The course aims to provide fundamental and advanced understanding of fluid mechanics.


Objectives
* This is a graduate/advanced undergraduate level course on Fluid Mechanics, from which the students are
* expected to gain valuable insights into various aspects of fluid motion, which are typically not disseminated in an undergraduate course. 
* An introductory turbulence will expose the students to some of the most complicated and fascinating phenomena in fluid dynamics. 
* These topics would provide the students with a strong platform to initiate research in this field and transport processes in general, where they are expected to apply many of the techniques and concepts acquired in this course.


Course contents
Essential Fundamentals: 
Review of vector calculus; Introduction to tensors; Brief discussions on Index Notation and Tensor Algebra/Calculus; The Continuum Hypothesis and Knudsen number; Eulerian and Lagrangian Description; Fluid Kinematics: Velocity field; Angular Deformation and Rate of Strain Tensor; Volumetric Deformation; Vorticity and Rate of Rotation Tensor; Irrotational flows; Stream Function; Velocity Potential; Elements of Potential flow theory.
The Fundamental Governing Equations - Differential and Integral Forms:
The Reynolds Transport Theorem - Derivation with simple examples; Conservation of Mass - overall and species mass; Conservation of Momentum; The Stress Tensor; The Traction Vector; The Cauchy Momentum Equation; Stresses in fluids - Deviatoric and Hydrostatic stresses; Constitutive Behavior and Stokes Hypothesis; The Navier-Stokes Equations and its physical interpretation; The Vorticity Transport Equation and its interpretation; Conservation of Energy; Governing equation for Mechanical Energy; Energy Equation - The Internal Energy form and the Enthalpy form; Physical Interpretation of the Energy Equation; Introduction to Boussinesq approximation and its applicability.
Solutions for Simple Flows: 
Analytical Solutions for Fully developed internal flows; Unidirectional Unsteady Flows; Fundamentals of Thermally developed flows - Convective Heat transfer coefficient and Nusselt Number; Essentials of Scaling analysis: Introduction to Order of Magnitude analysis; Characteristic Values of flow variables; Non-dimensional forms of the Governing Equations; Scaling of different terms in the Navier-Stokes and Energy Equations; Physical Interpretation of various non-dimensional numbers.
Hydrodynamic and Thermal Boundary Layers: 
Introduction to the Boundary Layer Approximation; Preliminary scaling analysis; Momentum and Energy Integral Equations; Similarity Solutions for Velocity and Temperature Fields - The Blasius Equation and its solution; Variations in Coefficient of friction, Convective Heat Transfer Coefficient and Nusselt Number; Role of Prandtl Number on the Thermal Boundary Layer; Falkner-Skan Similarity Solutions for Boundary Layers on a Wedge; Boundary Layer Separation and its implications - Increased Form Drag; Thermally developing flows and the Graetz Problem.
Reference texts:
* P. K. Kundu and I. M. Cohen, "Fluid Mechanics". 4th Edition, Academic Press San Diego, CA (2008).
* L. G. Leal, "Advanced transport phenomena: fluid mechanics and convective transport processes". Cambridge University Press (2007).
*  W. Kays, M. Crawford and B. Weigand (2017). Convective Heat and Mass Transfer. McGraw Hill.
* Batchelor, G. K. (1999). Introduction to fluid dynamics. Cambridge University Press (Indian edition).
* White, F. M. (2006). Viscous Fluid Flow. McGraw Hill.

Course content

riumequations, principalstressesandstressinvariants. AnalysisofDeformation: Lagrangian
and Eulerian description, finite strain, small deformation theory, principal strains and strain
invariants, compatibility conditions. Constitutive Theory: Generalized Hooke’s law, linear
elasticity relations, constitutive relations for orthotropic and anisotropic materials yield cri-

strain, Airy stress function, pressure vessels. Torsion: Non-prismatic sections, thick and

Overview
This course builds the fundamentals and principles of computer vision, then develops both classical and learning-based solutions across a wide range of applications. It begins with the mathematical groundwork and classical pipeline — image formation, features, and geometry — and moves into modern deep learning for vision, closing with advanced applications such as segmentation, depth estimation, neural radiance fields, and HDR imaging. Students from any discipline gain the foundational knowledge needed to build computer-vision models using OpenCV and PyTorch / Keras / TensorFlow.
Offered in Semester I of 2026–27 by Prof. Shanmuganathan Raman. Course materials, announcements, and assignments are managed through Google Classroom (join code dfrc4n7z).

The tools covered are intended to help students across disciplines who need the foundational knowledge to build computer-vision models using OpenCV and PyTorch / Keras / TensorFlow.

Lecture Schedule
The course runs as twenty-eight lecture hours across six parts — classical, proof-complete methods first (Parts I–IV), then learning-based vision (Parts V–VI), with ten vision applications solved first by hand and then learned. A single-view Shape-from-X supplement (Lecture 18a) extends Hour 18. Per-lecture slides appear in the Slides column as each topic is covered; the course frontmatter deck — roadmaps, notation and conventions for all twenty-eight hours — is available now.

Questions
Is there a final project?
No separate final project. Each of the three assignments is a substantial programming task, so you get project-scale practice throughout the semester.
How are assignments graded?
You submit code by the deadline, then take a short individual quiz or viva on your own submission. The viva is where the marks are decided: be ready to explain your code, your plots and your choices. See Grading.
Language and framework?
Python and PyTorch. No other frameworks (TensorFlow, JAX) unless explicitly allowed.
Do I need a GPU?
Not for everything, but some assignments benefit from one. A free Colab GPU is enough; any extra compute credits will be announced on Slack.
Where are the slides and notebooks?
In the lecture list: every lecture links its notes, slides, cheat sheet, notebooks and videos. The course materials site has the full set of decks, runnable notebooks and assignments.
Can I use AI tools?
Yes, honestly and with meaningful assistance documented. What is assessed is your ability to explain your own work in the viva, which no tool can do for you.
Anything else: ask on the course Slack.

ES 668 -  5G and Beyond: An introduction 


Intended Audience:  Advanced undergraduates (UG 3rd/4th Year) and graduate (PG 1st/2nd Year) students in Electrical Engineering, Computer Science and Engineering, Artificial Intelligence and allied disciplines. 


Learning outcomes.
1. Develop a use-case perspective of 5G in terms of data volume, latency, reliability etc. 
2. Develop familiarity with the evolution of 5G, terminologies, specifications and standards. 
3. Develop a deeper understanding of physical layer aspects of 5G new radio.


Module 1: Overview of 5G 
* Overview of 5G technology, its evolution and its significance in the telecommunications landscape.  Standardization organizations and their role in shaping 5G technology.
* Understanding the transformative potential of 5G in industries such as Internet of Things (IoT), augmented reality (AR), virtual reality (VR), autonomous systems, and connected transportation.
* 5G High-level architecture: Core network and radio access network (RAN). Protocol stack: Physical layer, MAC layer, RLC layer, PDCP layer, RRC layer, and others. User and control planes.


Module 2: 5G radio access network
* Spectra, antenna and radio propagation. Antenna arrays. Millimeter wave propagation loss, multipath fading and coherence. Modulation and demodulation. multiplexing and multiple access. OFDM, OFDMA. 5G-specific signal processing issues, power management, Error management.
* Multiple antenna techniques. Beam steering, Beam forming. Spatial multiplexing. MIMO and coherence, massive MIMO.
* 5G Radio interface. Air interface protocol stack. Frequency bands and combinations. frequency domain structure and numerologies. Time domain structure Transport channel, physical channel and analogue processing.


—------- midterm exams—-
Module 3: 5G and Virtualization
* Understanding the end-to-end 5G communication architecture. components of 5G.
* Software-Defined Networks - Architecture and Principles: SDN in mobile backhaul networks; SDN Control plane signaling. use cases and case studies in 5G/telecommunication networks.
* Understanding IPv6, Mobile IP, network virtualization and Network Function virtualization. ETSI NFV reference architecture, service management and orchestration in telecommunication networks. 
* Multi-access Edge computing in 5G and B5G networks: MEC Architecture, Deployment model, User mobility, session and service continuity, network traffic routing.
Module 4: Automation in 5G:
* Understanding of Network Slicing, Requirements for slice automation and 5G packet core services. End-2-End network slicing and service Assurances.
* Cloud RAN Architecture, challenges and Non-public 5G networks.
* Open Challenges and research prospects - Security, Scalability, Interoperability, Cell-Free communication and management. 


Evaluation criteria
1. In class quizzes, weekly, multiple choice
2. Pen and paper problems based assignments.
3. Class student presentations.
4. 5G simulation projects using tools like pyLTE, UERanSim, NS3.
5. Midterm and final exams - design problems.
6. Term Project with Hands-on experience with 5G applications, networking systems, communication protocol design. 


Lab Facilities and Resources: 5GLab


Background and prerequisites:  The course does not set hard prerequisites and will not assume prior knowledge. 


Justification and requirements of the course:  There is a need to provide a broad-based understanding of 5G and advanced mobile communication technologies to electrical engineering and computer science students at an introductory level without assuming deeper understanding of digital communications, wireless and optical systems and computer networks. 


Existing related courses on advanced mobile communications and advanced optical communications are aimed at electrical engineering students with a background course in analog and digital communications.
